commits.author: amd-pratmish
commits.message:
[levanter] Order multi-process checkpoint commits across NFS clients (#11620)

The lock files from #10969 stop two clients from committing at once, but
a
client can still open a directory entry cached from before another
client's
publish and rewrite an older manifest over it. Before each commit, the
writer
now refreshes the checkpoint directory and holds a commit-order lock
until the
commit finishes, so the next client rewrites the manifest the previous
one
published.

A save also publishes a writer lease for its lifetime. Process 0 removes
lock
files left by an interrupted save only when that lease is gone or stale,
so a
live writer keeps its lock.

Reading `zarr.json` back goes through the manifest without the lock and
failed
with `ESTALE` while another client replaced it. Two processes creating
the same
array metadata in concurrent transactions failed with `ALREADY_EXISTS`.
Process
0 now publishes the array metadata once and the other processes open
with it
instead of reading it back. A PyTree that is a single array has an empty
path
and stays at the database root; it was written under `/`, where restore
does
not look.

On two nodes of 8 MI355X with NFSv4.2 checkpoints, 140 multi-writer
saves had
no `ESTALE` failures against 3 of 194 on main, and every save restored
bitwise. Large saves took 8-12% longer (800 GiB: 851 s to 918 s).
Without
#11628, an 800 GiB save peaked at 233 GiB of host RAM on process 0
against 76
GiB on main; #11628 batches a large save into one manifest commit per
staging
wave and brings that back to main's level. Results:

https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11620#issuecomment-7115280819

commits.author: chrismc91
commits.message:
[eval] Save evaluation attempts larger than the store's batch limit (#12243)

A curated evaluation saves each finished attempt in one FineStore
commit: its attempt, sample and rollout rows plus the attempt blob. That
blob records every model request with its full message history, token
IDs and logprobs, so it grows with the square of an agent episode's
turns. A Muse Glimmer 30B run of SWE-Bench Pro's 200-task subset with
mini-swe-agent at a 131,072-token context (#11774) wrote one attempt
over the store's 100 MiB transaction limit. `TransactionTooLarge`
propagated out of `_save_attempt` and stopped the run after 76 of 200
tasks. Attempt blobs in its 22-task smoke run already reached 60 MB.

`_save_attempt` now commits through `DataStore.unbounded_transaction()`.
The limit caps batched writes, and an attempt is one record that cannot
be split across commits. The run object and appended rows keep the
bounded transaction. The regression test shrinks the store's limit to 64
KiB and checks that a larger reply is saved and graded; without the
change it fails with `TransactionTooLarge`.

An oversized attempt is held in memory while it commits, which the
writer's single thread bounds to one at a time. Storing each episode's
history once instead of per request would shrink these records and is
left for a separate change.

commits.author: chrismc91
commits.message:
[eval] Build evaluation task-machine factories when a task first needs one (#12218)

The evaluation worker defaults every run to a local verifier machine
(`execution_config`) and built every selected backend's factory before
the run started. `LocalMachineFactory` checks for Linux bubblewrap in
its constructor, so chat and LLM-judge evaluations, whose graders run in
process and never use a machine, failed at startup on macOS or any other
host without bubblewrap. That blocks running
`experiments.evaluation.task_driver --local` against a hosted endpoint
from a laptop, the fastest way to smoke a new benchmark.

`machine_factories` now returns a mapping that builds each backend's
factory the first time a task looks it up. The engine looks factories up
only in `validate_spec` for tasks whose episode or grader runs in a
machine, so in-process runs never construct one. On a host without
bubblewrap, an attempt whose task uses a local machine still fails
validation before its own generation and stops the run; machine-free
attempts already in flight finish first. The Daytona account is still
checked up front; only its factory waits.

A new test runs the driver's retry corpora with `LocalMachineFactory`
replaced by one that raises, and all eight attempts grade. Without this
change it fails at startup. On macOS the five `test_task_driver` tests
that previously failed with `SandboxUnavailable` now pass;
`test_trivial_replies` still needs Linux because its graders use
machines.

commits.author: penfever
commits.message:
[shellbox] Make the local machine keeper the sandbox's PID 1 (#12205)

Shellbox's local backend ran bwrap itself as the sandbox's PID 1 and the
machine's lifecycle keeper (`sleep 2147483647`) as PID 2. The native
root-delivery grading grader runs a quiesce as each grading collect's
first
command that kills every process outside its ancestry except PID 1, so
it
killed the keeper, bwrap exited 137, and the machine closed mid-grading.
Every local-tier attempt of a source still shipping that original
quiesce
died this way — 6,122+ unscored facet_v2 attempts in one day
(2026-11-24),
plus Cascade-2 and stem_mcqa failures.

The keeper's bwrap invocation now passes `--as-pid-1`. The payload is a
minimal init that owns PID 1 and keeps the sleeper `sleep 2147483647`
running as its child, so quiesces spare the machine by PID 1 and, where
they
also spare by exact argv, by the sleeper too; the init respawns the
sleeper
if anything kills it, so the failure cannot return. Because bwrap no
longer
runs its reaper, the init also reaps: guest processes orphaned inside
the
machine reparent to PID 1 and are collected when they die, so `kill -0`,
`/proc` and `pgrep` report a dead daemon as gone, as the Docker
backend's
`--init` does.

New behavior tests run the quiesce semantics (the grader's python3 form
and
its pure-shell form) against a real local machine with a stray for the
quiesce to kill, require the stray to be reaped, and require the machine
to
stay open afterwards; another collects a daemon orphaned by its
command's
exit, and one pins the sleeper to the guest init. They fail on the
previous
layout and pass with the fix, verified against real bwrap on Linux, with
the
reaper semantics verified under dash, busybox ash and bash as guest PID
1.
The same change is landed on the atlas-env-audit and
benfeuer/long-loop-prototype integration branches.

commits.author: ravwojdyla-agent
commits.message:
[rolloutengine] Write rollout events to Finelog (#11968)

Builds on #11940 (event order, time and attempt facts) and #11941
(larger client buffers and bounded sends). Design:
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WEs4GTqpNKC6P0ujncpJ7E1iOrzNCgFjlNmfBa3kWQE

`FinelogObserver` writes the events of a task attempt to two Finelog
tables. `rolloutengine.events` gets one row for each event, and
`rolloutengine.messages` one row for each transcript message. A task
attempt can then be read with SQL while it runs, across runs and
producers. Today a transcript is readable only after the attempt ends,
in the evaluation archive or in the sampled SkyRL trajectories. No
caller creates the observer yet.

The events table has every task attempt, and `content_fraction` is the
share of task attempts whose messages are written. Finelog is telemetry
here: rows can repeat or be lost, and the returned `Rollout` stays the
record. The tables register with a schema and no `TableSpec`, so
producers from different branches can write to one table.

On the dev cluster with the same observer code (at 091974f59c, before
the rebase), 200 task attempts wrote all 2,400 event rows, none
repeated. With `content_fraction=0.5`, 100 attempts wrote all 9 of their
message rows each, and a transcript read back from the tables was equal
to the returned rollout.

Open with the Finelog owner: the messages table repeats content that the
two stores above hold after the fact, which #9236 chose not to do in
Finelog. Capture rates, retention and the storage mode are open too.
Without a `TableSpec`, the hub misses the rows that a cluster wrote
before its forwarder first saw the table; with one, a branch that adds a
column conflicts.

Next: the SkyRL rollout worker creates the observer and gets a `follow`
command, then the evaluation worker.

[eval] Add the PDBThink coordinate benchmark (#11059)

Add `--evals pdbthink` to the native TaskCompendium evaluation catalog,
pinned to [upstream
`1bf06a4`](https://github.com/Open-Athena/pdbthink/tree/1bf06a464b2eab2f1e16c4dd16714314f225e196).
The published panel contains 88 coordinate questions in 19 families.
Three completions per question use temperature 0.7 and the remaining
model context. Headline accuracy weights families equally;
partial-credit scores remain available separately. Scoring uses the
pinned programmatic verifier, with no tools or LLM judge.

The shared launcher accepts a per-model `evaluation_request_timeout` and
extends evaluator and inference-transport deadlines together. Changing
only a candidate or judge deadline preserves launch, Harbor resume and
raw-archive identity, so interrupted runs can resume without
regenerating completed answers; token and turn budgets still belong to
scoring identity. The default deadline is omitted from recipe
fingerprints, and absent deadlines stay omitted from recorded model
configurations, preserving historical artifact hashes and policy
admission. Verified downloads use `StoragePath` for local and regional
object-storage URLs, while HTTP(S) downloads retain `requests` and its
60-second timeout; both paths verify SHA-256.

Chat protocols can select `provider_response` to pass the assistant
message and finish reason to the verifier, so PDBThink can reject
refusals, unexpected tool calls and truncated reasoning. The opt-in
`overflow="error"` context policy rejects an oversized cohort before
inference instead of excluding questions from its denominator. The
default policy stays omitted from serialization, preserving existing
corpus hashes. The `EVALUATION_EXECUTION_REVISION` bump intentionally
gives curated evaluations new run identities once, separating archives
produced under the changed response-grading behavior; subsequent
deadline changes alone preserve identity.

PDBThink adds reasoning over explicit 3D atom coordinates to the ID
suite: distances, contacts, residue environments, interfaces and
structural changes. This complements biomedical knowledge and text
questions such as PubMedQA/MedQA and the sequence tasks in GenomeQA. Its
value is coverage of this input and reasoning format; downstream
predictive validity has not been established. Treat the publicly
released panel as a development eval and exclude its questions and
completions from training.

The panel replaces the earlier 121-question/253-render candidate bundle.
It excludes mechanism tasks and the defective 7WZ5 glycosylation-clash
item. Fold-classification thresholds remain implicit in S05, and all
instances retain upstream `proposed` status. [The benchmark
guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/pdbthink-eval/docs/explanations/pdbthink.md)
describes the scientific limits, protocol and immutable data cache.

All 88 imported prompts and answer keys match upstream's published
artifacts. Replaying 1,512 selected responses reproduces their grades
and all 18 published model-condition accuracy bounds, retaining
incomplete coverage where upstream reports it. A full 88-response replay
also matches through the network-denied grader sandbox. [Replay
evidence](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fevaluation%2Fpdbthink%2Fnative-20261123%2Fvalidation%2F)
is retained with the run artifacts.

Both baselines scored all 264 completions (88 questions × 3), with zero
infrastructure errors. These use each model's full context allowance;
upstream's published conditions generally use one completion per
question.

Micro accuracy | Successful-run H100-hours |

| [Muse Glimmer
30B](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-rno2a%2Fmarin%2Fevaluation%2Fpdbthink%2Fnative-20261123%2Fmuse-baseline%2F)

[finelog] Upgrade DataFusion to 55 to restore pruning beside prefix LIKE (#11970)

Finelog now builds against DataFusion 55.3 (with datafusion-datasource
and datafusion-datasource-parquet at the same version), which pins Arrow
and Parquet 59.3. Each resolves to a single version in the lock. Segment
pruning again receives every pushed-down filter. #11857 limited it to
Int64 conjuncts because, before DataFusion 55, statistics pruning
rewrote a prefix `LIKE` into comparisons of a `Utf8View` column's bounds
with `Utf8` literals; those comparisons failed to evaluate, and the
failure turned off pruning for the whole predicate, time bounds
included.

DataFusion 55 opens Parquet files only through its Morsel API:
`ParquetSource::create_file_opener` now returns an internal error. The
indexed object-store scan opens a covering projection and falls back to
the source file, so it needs a per-file open. `MorselFileOpener`
provides one by driving the inner morselizer for each file in the order
`FileStream` uses (active reader, ready morsels, pending planner I/O,
ready planners), with one I/O outstanding at a time. The other changes
follow the 54 and 55 upgrade guides. In particular, `PartitionedFile`
extensions are now a typed map, and a file still carries only its newest
access plan.

A new test runs `worker_id LIKE 'w-%' AND timestamp_ms >= 2000`, and the
`starts_with` form, and reads the Parquet scan's metrics. It requires
zero predicate evaluation errors and the same row-group statistics
pruning as the time filter alone. In DataFusion 55, the pruning happens
at row-group level: file-range pruning keeps every file. On the
DataFusion 53 pins the test reports 11 evaluation errors.

Rollback to the previous build stays safe. The Parquet 59 writer
defaults match 58, apart from the new `write_path_in_schema`, which
defaults to the old behavior. A 2M-row corpus written by the new server
reads back through the previous server with identical results for all 12
benchmark queries. A standalone Parquet 58.3 reader also decodes every
segment file in full, including the page index.

## Performance

On Linux with jemalloc, the configuration that ships, DataFusion 55
matches 53. The table shows `log_query_bench measure` p50 in ms on one
2M-row corpus, copied fresh for each run, with 53 and 55 alternating
over two rounds. Every query returns identical results on both versions
and in every configuration. The Linux run used an x86_64 GCE worker with
an 8-CPU cgroup limit, where the server uses 16 partitions.

- "system allocator": the same server built without the jemalloc global

[evals] Add the ARC-AGI-2 public evaluation (#12149)

Add `arc-agi-2`: the 167 test inputs of the 120 public evaluation tasks
in [ARC-AGI-2](https://github.com/arcprize/ARC-AGI-2) @ `f3283f727488`,
read from the repository archive with a pinned SHA-256. Each task shows
a few input/output grid pairs, and the model must produce the output
grid for a new input. The prompt and answer extraction follow ARC
Prize's
[arc-agi-benchmarking](https://github.com/arcprize/arc-agi-benchmarking)
runner @ `78f2d3eacb86`: one prompt per test input with every training
pair, then the first `\boxed{...}` grid or else the last bracketed JSON
list of lists, which must equal the reference exactly. The runner's
fallback LLM extraction call is omitted. Grading sees the final answer
only. Each test input is sampled twice with the served model's defaults
and weighted by one over its task's test-input count, so `accuracy` is
task-averaged pass@1. ARC Prize reports pass@2 (a test input counts if
either attempt is correct); the trial records support it, but the shared
reducer does not compute it, so pass@2 below is computed offline. The
benchmark is in no suite. The dataset is Apache-2.0 and the runner is
MIT; the dataset README asks that the evaluation tasks not be used for
training.

Grid comparison uses verifyit's existing ARC-AGI-2 grader, so the grader
environment adds `jsonschema` and `pyyaml`. A grid with a NaN or
infinite cell scores zero as an invalid grid, and the verdict omits it,
because verdict details must be valid JSON.

Full runs on 2026-11-20 on CoreWeave H100s in `cw-rno2a`:

| Model | Hardware | Scored | pass@1 | pass@2 | Truncated | Published |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| muse-glimmer-30b | H100x2 | 334/334 | 9.7 ± 2.1 | 14.4 | 65 | |
| nvidia-nemotron-3.5-super-vl-120b-a12b-bf16 | H100x4 | 280/334 | 3.6 ±
1.5 | 3.9 | 113 | 1.9 (ARC Prize leaderboard, semi-private set) |
| Snowball v0.1 | H100x8 | 334/334 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 20 | |

Truncated and unparseable answers score zero. The protocol sets no
output cap, so the served model's context window bounds each answer (ARC
Prize's published runs set 100,000 tokens); the evaluator caps each
request at 1800 s. Nemotron's 54 unscored attempts hit that cap, so the
run ended as failed with their evidence saved; counting them as wrong
gives 3.1 pass@1. Re-grading every saved attempt offline with the
extraction code reproduced every recorded grade. Glimmer solved 22 of
120 tasks; 20 of them are also solved by ARC Prize's published GPT-5.4
run. 178 of Snowball's 334 attempts give a wrong grid of the right
dimensions, and 36 copy the test input.

As a reference check, Kimi K2.5 ran through OpenRouter on the first 20
test inputs (an API smoke run, not a full run; [ARC Prize's published
Kimi K2.5
run](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arcprize/arc_agi_v2_public_eval)
scores 8.75 pass@1 and 12.08 pass@2 on the full set). On the 17 inputs
with graded attempts, all 17 compiled prompts match the prompts in ARC

commits.message:
[finestore] Add transactional table creation, rename, and drop (#12203)

Give FineStore transactions a private table namespace. Transactions
can create a table, stream its Parquet shards, and rename or drop
tables. A rename moves manifest references. The final names and other
writes publish under one HEAD update.

Build evaluation rollouts by staging a private table, renaming it into
place, and publishing its completion object in the same commit.
Commit guards reject concurrent changes to the source and destination
contents while allowing compaction.

Bind samples v4 backup and drop to the same exact file set. A drop
clears the archive seal. Renaming, replacing, or dropping an existing
table fences append handles registered under its earlier incarnation.
A store must flush its buffered appends before resetting a registered
table.
After publication it can register a fresh handle for that name.

First table publications keep the existing manifest requirements.
An incarnation change requires the `table-incarnations-v1` feature.
Upgrade readers such as Marina's EvalDash before deploying writers
that reset existing tables.

### Table DDL and failed publication

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    BASE["Pin a base manifest"] --> DDL["Create, rename, or drop tables in the private namespace"]
    DDL --> SHARDS["Stream new rows to immutable Parquet shards"]
    DDL -->|No new rows| GUARDS
    SHARDS --> GUARDS["Check affected tables and declared dependencies"]
    GUARDS -->|Checks pass and writes are pending| MANIFEST["Write a manifest with final table names, shard references, and object writes"]
    GUARDS -->|No writes on an existing archive| CHECKED["Return the checked commit token"]
    MANIFEST --> PUBLISH{"Advance HEAD with compare-and-swap"}
    PUBLISH -->|Success| VISIBLE["New readers see the entire commit"]
    PUBLISH -->|Another writer advanced HEAD| RETRY["Reload HEAD"]
    RETRY --> GUARDS
    SHARDS -->|Creator exits while staging| ABORT["This transaction leaves HEAD untouched"]
    MANIFEST -->|Creator exits before publication| ABORT
    GUARDS -->|Conflict| ABORT
    ABORT --> ORPHANS["Unpublished shards or manifests can remain in storage"]
```

Existing readers keep their pinned manifest. Once `HEAD` advances, the
new
snapshot is visible even if the creator exits before receiving its
commit token.
Staging reclamation is separate maintenance. A collector needs to fence
abandoned transactions and preserve shard paths referenced by retained
manifests.

[grug] Fix MuonH grouping for stacked experts (#11639)

Route stacked expert matrices to MuonH and norm weights to Adam.
Four-dimensional expert updates use hero-EP's Newton–Schulz and
hyperball implementation; the 10/05 generic backend passed 4-D
directions through without Newton–Schulz; two- and three-dimensional
leaves retain the generic backend. Their orthogonalisation has the same
mathematical purpose as hero-EP's, though the sharded implementations
differ. The affected runs are recorded in [issue
11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535#issuecomment-6963588890).

The optimizer defaults to per-expert normalization and no global
clipping. The long-loop spec follow-up must explicitly select
`all_experts`, `global_grad_norm: 1.0`, and `use_syrk: true` for Mochi's
settings. Global clipping preserves the top-level optimizer state and
cannot be combined with per-group clipping. The generic and June TPU
optimizer modules register identical names and cannot be imported
together; the long-loop runtime imports
`experiments.grug.moe.optimizer`.

Two runs with experts in MuonH on the 64-H100 data8 long-loop layout did
not finish their first step; ~~the cause is under diagnosis.~~ The
long-loop SFT runtime needs a follow-up before this grouping is used at
scale.

The sharded 4-D parity test passed locally with two CPU devices; CI
normally runs it on one CPU device.

---

shard the layer axis over spare intra-rack axes (with padding when not

and the `expert=2, context=1, data=2` hero layout.

commits.message:
[iris] Skip runsc log redirection when the config disables logging (#12223)

The node agent's runtime-storage init container now leaves
`/etc/containerd/runsc.toml` untouched when the file sets neither
`log_path` nor `runsc_config.debug-log`, and makes that decision before
checking the NVMe mount. A config that sets either key still goes
through the existing redirection to NVMe, which fails fast unless both
are present, and a `runsc_config` that is not a table is rejected.

CoreWeave node images are moving to a release that provides the
`cw-kata-qemu` runtime Iris sandboxes are switching to (#11841). That
release ships `runsc.toml` with both log settings commented out, so
gVisor shims log through containerd and nothing reaches the RAM-backed
root filesystem that #11079 protected. The init container required
exactly one `log_path` line, raised `ValueError: Expected one log_path
setting in runsc config; found 0` on these images, and kept the node
agent from starting, which removed node telemetry, cache reclaim and
storage-health probes from updated nodes. The new test uses that file
verbatim.

Incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/1062

[ci] Run unit legs on every vCPU with a job-local JAX cache (#11906)

pytest `-n auto` counts physical cores, so each 4-vCPU hosted runner ran
2 xdist workers. `-n logical` runs 4. Each unit leg also sets a JAX
persistent compilation cache in the runner's temp directory, so xdist
workers and tests reuse compiled programs within the job.

Together the two changes cut the levanter and marin shards' total test
time by about 30%. Each shard ran every configuration in sequence on one
runner, because hosted runners come from several CPU models whose speed
differs by up to 2x on the same shard. The runs are on the Open-Athena
fork:
[workers](https://github.com/Open-Athena/marin/actions/runs/44826067851)
and
[cache](https://github.com/Open-Athena/marin/actions/runs/44830910208).

| Change | Slowest shard before, s | Slowest shard after, s | Total over
8 shards before, min | Total after, min | Change in total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 → 4 workers | 407 | 342 | 35.3 | 28.4 | −20% |
| Job-local cache, at 4 workers | 286 | 268 | 28.8 | 25.2 | −12% |

Peak memory reached 7.4 GB of the runners' 16 GB, with no swap. In an
earlier trial,
`test_stream_response_cleans_up_when_http_delivery_stops[deadline]`
timed out once at 4 workers; it passed in the other 11 four-worker runs
of its shard.

The cache is not saved between jobs. JAX's cache keys differ by host
CPU, and a runner that restored another runner's cache recompiled every
entry when the CPUs differed. The trial's 55 runners came from 9 CPU
variants, so one saved cache would match the next runner 18% of the
time.

Every unit leg gets 4 workers, including scopes the trial did not
measure. This PR's CI runs all of them because it changes the selector.

[skyrl] Adopt the vLLM wheel with batch-invariant NCCL algorithms (#12185)

SkyRL installs a vLLM wheel whose batch-invariant mode keeps NCCL's Ring
and Tree algorithms enabled, so vLLM engine processes can run AllGather
under NCCL 2.32.6. The wheel is
[marin-vllm-gpu-20261124-7e9b413a5daf](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/releases/tag/marin-vllm-gpu-20261124-7e9b413a5daf);
its initializer sets `NCCL_ALGO=ring,tree;allreduce:tree`
(marin-community/vllm#139), the value SkyRL's learner and Ray workers
use, so the learner takes the value from the initializer. The previous
wheel's initializer set `NCCL_ALGO=allreduce:tree`, which leaves
AllGather without an algorithm under NCCL 2.32.6, and the GPU nightly's
disaggregated rollout test failed with `NCCL error: invalid usage`.

The wheel also carries the fork's GrugMoE and speculative-decoding
changes since the previous pin: full decode graphs and GB200 expert GEMM
tuning, Triton MoE workspace reservation, padding-logit clearing before
expert selection, ShortConv output writes, dense speculative drafts kept
out of expert-parallel groups, and DSpark serving for Grug drafts. The
release passed the fork's H100 and GB200 wheel qualification. In
`vendor/skyrl/uv.lock` only the `vllm` entries change, and `uv lock
--check` passes.

The [SkyRL GPU nightly on this
branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/45365513133)
passed all three H100 lanes, including the Grug Megatron suite and its
disaggregated rollout test. Snowball `eval-short` on eight H100s scored
all 1,500 EvalLite tasks with a mean of 0.588; the previous wheel scored
0.555 on the same model and tasks before grader changes on main, so the
two are not directly comparable. Mochi `train-medium` on 15 nodes of
four GB200s completed both updates from the step-400407 Mochi SFT
checkpoint.

Fixes #11955

[evals] Add IMO-ProofBench with a GLM-5.3-Flash judge (#11967)

Add IMO-ProofBench (60 olympiad proofs, 30 Basic and 30 Advanced, 4
trials) to the curated evals, graded by GLM-5.3-Flash on Together with
the paper's ProofAutoGrader prompt. The judge awards 7, 6, 1 or 0 points
and the score is points over 7. Data and prompt are CC BY 4.0 from
google-deepmind/superhuman, pinned by commit and sha256. IMO-AnswerBench
was added in #11764.

The judge was chosen on IMO-GradingBench, the paper's 1000 human-graded
ProofBench responses, using 200 of them (50 per grade class) and this
prompt:

| Judge | Accuracy | MAE | Bias | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GLM-5.3-Flash | 63.5% [57.5, 69.5] | 18.7% | under-grades Almost (−1.3
points) | $3.96 |
| gpt-oss-120b | 53.5% [48.0, 59.0] | 21.6% | over-grades Partial (+0.9
points) | $0.28 |

published vanilla-prompt result is o3 at 54.0% accuracy and 20.2% MAE.
On a Muse Glimmer 30B smoke run (PB-Basic-001..020, 4 trials) GLM scored
65.4% where gpt-oss-120b scored 89.3%.

judge therefore keeps Together's default sampling, through

gave every grade a fixed 600 s, so a judge spec could not declare a

deadline, and the attempt deadline grows by the same amount. ProofBench
declares 900 s requests within 1200 s. IMO-AnswerBench's judge already
declared 900 s and now gets it.

commits.author: XiaoyuanWang111
commits.message:
[eval] Regrade stored model responses on republished corpora (#11223)

Add `--responses-from` to `experiments.evaluation.task_driver`, so a run
on republished corpora can grade the model responses that an earlier run
stored instead of sampling new ones. A grader correction changes corpus
identity, so the old result root cannot be resumed, and a new run would
sample every response again. With `run_evaluation(...,
reuse_from=ROOT)`, each generation attempt takes the latest completed
response that `ROOT` stored for the same benchmark, source row and
trial, provided the attempt sends the identical request: messages,
sampling options and trial seed. Every other attempt asks the endpoint,
so a regrade takes `--config` and an endpoint as any run does. Resume
already reuses a completed response when only grading failed, and
`reuse_from` applies the same completed-response rule to another result
root. The new corpus's response policy selects the graded text from the
stored content and reasoning fields.

The source root must hold a run with the same `ModelIdentity`, or the
run refuses to start. Each reused attempt's raw evidence records the
source root, its run identity and the evidence blob in
`reused_response_from_run`, and the attempt records zero tokens, as
attempts that reuse their own response after a grading failure already
do. `evaluation/run.json` lists each source in `response_sources` with
its root, run identity and `driver_revision`, so a regraded root differs
from a fresh run on the same corpus without opening the evidence. The
reuse checks only model identity, so responses stored under another
driver revision are graded under the current one, and the recorded
revision shows it. The sources are outside the run identity: a resume
that names no source keeps the list, and one that names another source
adds to it.

Stored responses are looked up by benchmark, source row and trial
because the trials of an unseeded protocol send identical requests:
AIME25 and AMC23 run 10 trials without a seed, and JEEBench runs 3.
`marin.rollouts.evaluation.run_identity` holds the identity that resume
compares, which leaves out request concurrency and the response sources.
The resume check and the reuse provenance both call it, so a source run
resumed at another concurrency keeps the identity its regrades recorded.

Comparing a regraded root with its source, by `terminal_attempts` and
the metrics the protocol declares, is left to a follow-up in
`evalrecords`.

The change was validated on 1,600 stored CruxEval responses from
Snowball v0.1, regraded without calling the model, on 125fdde2d merged
with #11408 (main graded no CruxEval attempt until #11408 fixed #11404).
On the corpus they were first graded on, all 1,600 grades were
reproduced, and on the corpus published after #10970, 40 grades rose and
none fell. The source and regrade roots are in
[xiaoyuanwang/marin-11223-cruxeval-regrade](https://huggingface.co/datasets/xiaoyuanwang/marin-11223-cruxeval-regrade/tree/b71e737a5e97c2c55713f04d02a289ff72e06a13).
On the current CruxEval corpus, a regrade of the same source root also
reused all 1,600 responses with zero tokens and sent no request to the
endpoint.

commits.message:
[finestore] Record author and message on transaction commits (#12177)

DataStore.transaction and unbounded_transaction take an optional message
and author. With a message, the commit the transaction publishes records
them in its manifest as commit_info, with the commit's sequence and
publication time. ReadView.commit_info returns the record of the pinned
commit. A shared store edited by many people, such as a task pool, needs
this to show who changed a row and why.

The author defaults to the launching user through a new
rigging.provenance.launch_user(): the built_by published in
MARIN_PROVENANCE when present, else the OS login. An Iris worker
therefore records the submitting user rather than root. username_segment
now uses the same function. FineStore stores the author as given and
does not verify it.

commit_info describes only the commit that writes it. Each manifest is
copied from its parent, so every commit sets the field, to None when it
has no message. Older FineStore versions keep unknown manifest fields
when they copy a manifest, so their commits carry the parent's record
forward. The record names the sequence of its own commit, and
ReadView.commit_info ignores a record whose sequence differs from the
manifest's.

commits.author: XiaoyuanWang111
commits.message:
[eval] Score trivial replies through the evaluation driver (#11222)

Add `python -m experiments.evaluation.trivial_replies`, which reports what a benchmark's graders give to replies that ignore the task: the empty string, `hello`, `0`, `I don't know.` and the request's last user message. Each reply is passed to `run_evaluation` in place of the model, under the run configuration of the model run to compare with, so cohort selection, prompt variants, response selection, grading and grading retries are those of that run. The launcher runs on the host, as `task_driver --local` does, writes one FineStore archive per reply, and prints each benchmark's primary metric per reply. The table reduces each archive with `benchmark_scores`, split out of `score_curated_record` in `evalrecords`, so both read a result root the same way.

Evaluation publication grades no replies, so nothing shows what a short reply earns before a model is scored. On Marin's canonical IFBench corpus, built from its declaration at 4e4a35f8a and run with local bubblewrap machines under a 32,768-token context window, `hello` passes 121 of 300 prompts (0.403 strict prompt accuracy), `0` passes 103, `I don't know.` 57, the repeated prompt 40 and the empty reply none. On IFEval's canonical corpus, the repeated prompt passes 134 of 541 prompts (0.248), `0` passes 96, `I don't know.` 65, `hello` 62 and the empty reply none.

A reply is graded as written. A JSON-value answer format parses the whole reply as one JSON value, so the `json_*` replies submit the same text as a JSON string; no importer builds that format yet. The driver refuses corpora scored by likelihood or graded by a judge, because the launcher supplies neither a scorer nor a judge. A reply is not cut at the output budget, and its attempts record zero tokens.

[eval] Add MedMCQA likelihood and chain-of-thought benchmarks (#11843)

Add MedMCQA ([Pal et al., 2022](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v174/pal22a.html)) to the curated catalog as two benchmarks. MedMCQA has four-option questions from Indian medical entrance exams in 21 subjects. Both benchmarks score the 4,183-question validation split of [`openlifescienceai/medmcqa`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openlifescienceai/medmcqa) at `91c6572c454088bf71b679ad90aa8dffcd0d5868`, as lm-eval-harness does; the test split's answers are hidden (`cop = -1`). The dataset is Apache-2.0 on the Hub and MIT on GitHub; the lm-eval prompts are MIT. Neither benchmark is added to a suite.

`medmcqa` is lm-eval's zero-shot `medmcqa` task: the log-likelihood of the letters A to D after the question and lettered options. `medmcqa-cot` is lm-eval's `medmcqa_cot` chat prompt. It grades the first `Final Answer: X` in the final answer, where X is a standalone letter, through a new verifyit extraction, `McqExtraction.MEDMCQA_COT_REFERENCE`, beside SuperGPQA's. Prompts follow lm-eval at [`d6de816`](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/tree/d6de81643928d653435c431bae19945d41d32520/lm_eval/tasks/medmcqa). `medmcqa-cot` differs from the reference in four settings. It uses each model's token budget instead of 512 tokens, which would truncate reasoning models. It uses each model's default sampling instead of greedy decoding. It grades only the final answer, so a "Final Answer" line inside the reasoning does not count. It requires the letter to stand alone, where lm-eval's regex reads `Final Answer: Bone marrow` as B.

Marin's only MedMCQA coverage was the uncurated lm-eval pass-through in `experiments/evals/task_configs.py`. PubMedQA was the only curated medical benchmark.

| Model | Benchmark | Hardware | Scored | Score ± SE | Hit token budget | No answer | Reference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | `medmcqa-cot` | H100x4 | 4,183 / 4,183 | 81.35 ± 0.60 | 3 | 4 | none at this setting |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | `medmcqa-cot` | H100x2 | 4,183 / 4,183 | 76.48 ± 0.66 | 0 | 1 | none at this setting |
| Snowball Smartie RL step14 | `medmcqa-cot` | H100x8 | 4,183 / 4,183 | 74.04 ± 0.68 | 0 | 6 | none at this setting |
| Qwen3-0.6B | `medmcqa` | H100x1 | 4,183 / 4,183 | 32.30 ± 0.72 | n/a | n/a | lm-eval `medmcqa`, same model: 31.91 ± 0.72 |

Every compiled request for both benchmarks matches lm-eval's rendering of the same 4,183 rows. For `medmcqa`, lm-eval at `d6de816` ran Qwen3-0.6B (`c1899de`) in float32 on CPU. Its logged requests are identical to Marin's, and the two runs pick the same answer on 97.47% of questions (4,077). Each of the 106 disagreements is a near-tie in lm-eval's own scores: the gap between its top two answers has a median of 0.049 nats and a maximum of 0.31. Marin serves the model in bf16 on vLLM. Its per-choice log-likelihoods differ from lm-eval's by 0.055 nats on average and 0.42 at most. Options are not shuffled, and A is the gold answer for 32.2% of questions (B 25.9%, C 22.1%, D 19.7%), so answering A every time scores 32.2% on either benchmark. Qwen3-0.6B scores at that level without favoring A: it picks D for 49% of questions and A for 20%. Its run checks parity with lm-eval, not medical knowledge.

For `medmcqa-cot`, no published score matches this setting for a model Marin serves. All 60 responses from 20-question smoke runs on the three chat models were read with the reasoning separated from the final answer. Every grade is correct, and the answer key is correct on the 4 questions the models missed. In the full runs, 7 of the 11 unparsed answers come from a model that ended its turn without closing its reasoning, so the final answer is empty and scores 0. Counting them would add 0.10 points for Snowball and 0.02 for Nemotron. 3 are Nemotron responses that hit the 73.5k-token budget. The last is a Snowball response that answered `Final Answer: ABCD`; lm-eval's regex reads it as A, the gold answer. The full runs were graded by an evalchemy scorer with lm-eval's regex, before the grader moved to verifyit. Their table scores are rescored with the standalone-letter rule, which changes only that Snowball response; no other response in the three chat runs has an answer letter followed by a letter or digit. A 20-question Glimmer smoke through the verifyit grader scored all 20 questions at 85%, and each extracted letter matches the response's `Final Answer` line.

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-0.6B, `medmcqa` | H100x1 | 52 min | 54 min | 0.9 | 6 |
| Muse Glimmer 30B | H100x2 | 55 min | 58 min | 1.9 | 12 |
| Snowball Smartie RL step14 | H100x8 | 88 min | 59 min | 7.8 | 48 |
| Nemotron 3.5 Super | H100x4 | 174 min | 73 to 175 min | 4.9 to 11.7 | 30 to 72 |

[evals] Add IMO-AnswerBench (#11764)

Add IMO-AnswerBench from Google DeepMind's
[IMO-Bench](https://imobench.github.io) ([Luong et al., EMNLP
2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.01846), CC BY 4.0) as
`imo-answerbench`. It has 400 olympiad problems with short answers, 100
each in algebra, combinatorics, geometry and number theory, imported
from `answerbench_v2.csv` in
[google-deepmind/superhuman](https://github.com/google-deepmind/superhuman)
at `9b620a92` with a SHA-256 pin. The solver sees only the problem
statement, thinks with the model's served sampling defaults, and runs 4
trials per problem. The judge receives only the final message content,
never a separate reasoning field. The benchmark joins no suite.

The judge is `openai/gpt-oss-120b` on Together. It uses the paper's
AnswerAutoGrader prompt (appendix A.5), transcribed from the LaTeX
source. The paper's published scores used Gemini 2.5 Pro as the judge,
so our scores are comparable only between runs that share a judge. The
paper averages 8 runs on AnswerBench; this protocol runs 4. We changed
two things. The source filter drops `algebra-036` before conversion. Its
CSV columns are shifted: its short answer is "Algebra" and its category
is "Functional Equation". That leaves 399 problems. The answer grader
also gains one rule: a solution that offers more than one candidate
final answer without committing to one is incorrect. The prompt leaves
that case undefined, and Muse Glimmer 30B hedged in 8–16% of the
attempts we read.

| Model | Hardware | Attempts | Accuracy (95% CI) | Algebra | Comb. |
Geometry | Number theory | Ran out of tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muse Glimmer 30B | H100x2, 73.7K context | 1,600 | 80.2% ± 3.2 | 84.1
| 62.5 | 89.0 | 86.0 | 7 |
| Snowball v0.1 (Smartie RL step 14) | H100x8, 73.7K context | 1,600 |
50.4% ± 4.3 | 56.6 | 28.7 | 55.7 | 61.3 | 6 |

Both full runs used the AnswerBench grader as it was before this PR's
two changes: all 400 rows, and no hedging rule. Intervals are clustered
by problem. On Glimmer's run we audited the judge with a blinded review.
Opus and Fable each labelled a stratified sample of 118 attempts without
seeing any verdict, and their leans agreed on 95.8% of cases (Cohen's κ
0.905). The judge disagreed with their consensus on 2.4% of verdicts
[0.7, 5.3], or 1.0% on cases both reviewers called definite. Correcting
for those errors gives 78.6% [75.8, 80.3]. Most errors were hedged
answers, which the new rule addresses. Re-running the same judge flipped
1.1% of verdicts. A second judge, DeepSeek V4 Pro, scored 80.0% on the
1,505 attempts it could grade, where gpt-oss-120b scored 80.8%. On
Snowball, no boxed answer that matches the reference after whitespace
and LaTeX normalization was graded wrong.

Snowball needs `reasoning_parser: grug`. The September 25 campaign
config for this checkpoint keeps the reasoning in the message content
(`skip_special_tokens: false`). In that setup the judge read the full
reasoning, a median of 33K characters, and marked 5 of 80 smoke-run
answers wrong although each one matched the reference. With the parser,
the graded text is a median of 22 characters, and the smoke-run score
rose from 33.8% to 45%.

Nemotron 3.5 Super has no full run. In smoke runs on 20 problems, 182 of
the 185 attempts that finished were graded correct. Its median attempt
used 61K tokens, and many run past 100K. At 73.7K context, 36 of 80
attempts ran out of tokens. At 128K context with 64 concurrent requests,
35 of 80 attempts hit the eval stack's fixed 30-minute request limit
(`EVALUATION_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`). With 16 concurrent requests, 16
hit the limit and 10 more ran out of tokens at 128K. A valid Nemotron
score needs a longer request limit, faster decoding such as the MTP
speculative decoding in NVIDIA's serving recipe, and more than 128K
tokens of context.

IMO-ProofBench is left out. Its 20-problem smoke run on Glimmer scored
89.3% under an unaudited judge, and scores near 90% from an LLM proof
grader need a stronger judge, which the paper's IMO-GradingBench can
help choose.

| Run | Hardware | Wait | Eval time | Start to finish | Accelerator
hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Glimmer, AnswerBench full | H100x2 | ~4 min | 2 h 52 min | 3 h 1 min |
~6 H100-h |
| Snowball, AnswerBench full | H100x8 | queued for capacity and
preempted | 18 min after the last restart | 3 h 50 min | ≤ 31 H100-h |

Judge cost was not measured.

[rl] Check rollout worker CPU requests during planning (#11806)

A rollout pool can remain unscheduled when its pinned workers request
more CPUs than the driver task.

Check the worker count times its CPUs per worker against the driver
task's Iris CPU request during preset composition. The shared
driver-validation config does not contain that request. `--plan` and
host-side submissions reject oversized pools before GPU submission.
Static preference training with `trainer.evaluation_runner=training`
skips the check because it starts no inference rollout pool. Remove the
runtime Ray-node check.

Read-only records show that Ray advertised more CPUs than Iris
requested. The per-node averages were 144 versus a 120-CPU request in
`cw-us-east-08a`, 128 versus 32 in `cw-rno2a`, and 128 versus 16 in
`cw-us-east-02a`. No reserved-CPU deduction was observed. The plan uses
the Iris request as the conservative limit.

commits.author: XiaoyuanWang111
commits.message:
[agents] Settle audit-grader's replacement rule and rerun it on IFBench (#11218)

Step 3 of `audit-grader` now requires a replacement grader when a
fixture or a later step shows a defect that a change to the grader's
code can fix. For an LLM judge, that is a defect in a deterministic
stage; a defect in the judge model or its template is a finding. An
audit that finds no such defect needs none, and step 6 says how it
estimates the error rate of the grader alone: it stratifies the review
sample against the reference, or by the grader's own verdict when there
is no reference, and sizes each stratum for the interval that the
recommendation needs. A first round without a replacement may draw from
the whole panel, but it leaves responses unused in case it shows the
first defect that calls for one. Before, the skill described the
replacement in conditional terms while step 6 stratified by the
replacement's verdicts.

Step 6 also widens the interval of a grader that has no error in a
stratum's sample. Such a stratum adds zero to every bootstrap resample,
so the interval left out the errors that the sample could have missed.
In simulated reviews, the merged rule's 95% interval held the true rate
in 38% to 94% of reviews over 17 settings with stratum error rates of
0.5% to 5%: the strata of the IFBench audit's two review rounds, and two
label strata of 100 or 150 cases each. The upper end now rises by each
such stratum's share of the population times the exact 95% limit for no
error in n cases, with a Bonferroni correction when several strata have
no error, and the interval holds the true rate in 93% to 100% of the
same reviews.

`references/validation.md` reports a blind rerun on IFBench. A fresh
agent session audited Marin's vendored IFBench grader with SKILL.md and
the reviewer prompt as merged in #10422, without `references/ifbench.md`
or any result of the earlier IFBench audit, and two more sessions
reviewed its frozen sample of 458 verdicts. Of the earlier audit's 43
checker findings, the rerun reports 31 as findings and 8 as decision
entries, and misses 4. Every counterexample it gives reproduces on the
grader; 5 of its findings are defects that the earlier audit missed, and
8 are behaviors that the earlier audit or the rerun's reviewers treat as
decisions. It puts the grader's error rate at 7.2% [5.9, 9.1], against
7.6% [4.7, 11.3] and 6.1% [3.9, 10.1] in the earlier audit's two rounds,
and also recommends fixing the grader. This is one run, with one model
as auditor and reviewers; `validation.md` lists the other limits. The
run's files and the score card are in
[`audit-grader-suite`](https://github.com/XiaoyuanWang111/audit-grader-suite/tree/f4738d6ca7a3cb82a922232358962f371608e2e3).

#11187 tracks the two gaps in the skill that the rerun shows, and a loop
for recording such misses after each audit.

commits.message:
[verifyit] Reject partially parsed math references (#11989)

Reject math references and LIST members unless the whole normalized
LaTeX expression parses. The previous math-verify path could fall back
to a bare number, recover the last equation after a parse failure, or
select an inner math fragment. Unit normalization could also discard
terms after a `\text{...}` group. Long standalone prose groups remain
invalid; short text answers, escaped dollar amounts, connector groups,
and powered terminal units remain parseable. TaskCompendium converts
invalid references to `invalid_reference` instead of grading against a
fragment.

Use each reference member's unit normalization policy for its matching
candidate. A symbolic reference such as `2 s` matches the identical
answer without matching `2`; candidates with units match numeric
references when default normalization leaves the reference unchanged.
Terminal `\text{ m}` and `\mathrm{~cm}` units retain their unit
handling. Text groups that begin a math term, such as `\mathrm{x}`
inside a fraction, remain symbolic. Candidate answer extraction is
unchanged.

The [frozen-set
audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11989#issuecomment-7113679024)
found that head `8f6000def` reduced `MarinSkyRL:math500` from 500 to 487
problems: 8 short text answers, 3 escaped dollar amounts, and 2 powered
units. On those 13 dropped problems, 73 of 91 stored replies from seven
models scored 1.0 on main. The same head flipped 8 other stored
unit-bearing replies from 1.0 to 0.0. The audited parsing and
unit-policy edits restore these reference and reply shapes.

Under the current antlr 4.11 pin, 15,861 percentage-reference rows
remain rejected until #11938 lands. Merge this PR after or together with
#11938.

Fixes #11973

[execution] Preserve fingerprints for opt-in dataclass fields (#12078)

Mark an opt-in dataclass field with `fingerprint_omit_value` to keep the
fingerprint for its legacy behavior. For example, a kernel field marked
with the legacy value `"native"` is omitted when it selects the native
kernel. If its default changes to `"fixed"`, recipes that inherit the
new default get a new fingerprint. Recipes that explicitly select the
native kernel keep their fingerprint.

HF-to-Levanter conversion hashes the config with legacy values omitted
and sends the complete resolved config to the worker. The worker
receives the selected value even when the fingerprint omits it.

[iris] Pin the cw-us-east-02a controller to host g5bea54 (#12157)

Pin the cw-us-east-02a Iris controller to host g5bea54 instead of
g530e1c.

CoreWeave cordoned g530e1c on 2026-11-23 at 17:15 UTC after a
`KernelDeadlock` condition (CPU soft lockup) and marked it pending
`production-reboot`. The running controller pod survived the cordon, but
a controller restart at 21:18 UTC deleted it and the replacement stayed
`Pending`: the hostname selector admits only g530e1c, and the scheduler
rejects a cordoned node. The cluster had no controller for about 16
minutes.

The controller was redeployed with this pin at 21:34 UTC. g5bea54 is in
the same `cpu-genoa` scale group and had no controller state, so startup
restored the latest remote checkpoint, `controller-state/1795468673780`,
written at 21:17:53 UTC. Submissions accepted between that checkpoint
and the stop at 21:18:33 UTC are not in the restored database.

g530e1c still holds the previous local database under
`/mnt/local/iris-controller-state`. Moving the pin back after the node
reboots would restore from the remote checkpoint unless that copy's
checkpoint marker matches it, as described in [controller
state](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/docs/coreweave.md#controller-state).

[eval] Run Harbor agentic benchmarks from curated TaskSpec corpora (#11664) Marin's canonical agentic evaluations run curated TaskSpec corpora through `marin.rollouts.evaluation`. This covers the default agentic suite, its catalog variants, and the six active agentic evaluations in the September 25 campaign. FinanceAgent and standalone OT-TBLite have ingestion rules and stay outside the default suites. ```mermaid flowchart LR pkg["Harbor package
(HF commit or registry hash)"] --> imp["taskcompendium.importers.harbor
+ ingestion rule in agentic.py"] imp --> corpus["TaskSpec corpus
(digest-pinned images)"] corpus --> eval["marin.rollouts.evaluation"] eval --> engine["RolloutEngine
Terminus-2 / Pi / mini-swe-agent"] engine <--> machine["Shellbox machine
(Daytona)"] engine --> grade{"grader placement"} grade --> agentm["agent's machine
(tests/test.sh)"] grade --> fresh["fresh grader machine"] grade --> host["host: exact match or judge"] agentm & fresh & host --> records["FineStore run records"] ``` `taskcompendium.importers.harbor` lowers a pinned Harbor package to a TaskSpec without importing Harbor. It reads `task.toml` schemas 1.0 and 1.1, pins Dockerfile `FROM` lines and prebuilt images to digests, and turns Compose sidecars into task-machine services. Each dataset's ingestion rule chooses its grader: the package's `tests/test.sh`, or a captured answer graded on the host by exact match or a judge. A rule can also edit its packages before lowering; FinanceAgent's replace LiteLLM, which has had compromised PyPI releases, with the OpenAI SDK in its image and `retrieve_information` tool. TaskSpec schema 0.31 adds grader placement: in the agent's machine after its processes stop, which is Harbor's order, or in a fresh machine. Version 0.30 specs upgrade on load. `rolloutengine.agents` carries Harbor's Terminus-2, Pi and mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 with their prompts, parsers and terminal handling unchanged. A Shellbox adapter replaces Harbor's environment, and the engine's model client replaces LiteLLM, so every turn is recorded. Replay fixtures recorded from vendored Harbor check that the lifted agents send Harbor's requests and commands. As in Harbor, a timeout, context overflow, or an agent that exits its terminal ends the attempt and the engine grades the work left in the machine. Lost sandboxes, gateway and transfer failures, and setup failures are retryable infrastructure errors. Each harness revision is part of a run's identity. Each campaign recipe pins the packages of the campaign's `marin-community/harbor@38742b0f` registry. `evaluations.yaml` (formerly `evalchemy.yaml`) selects every evaluation, and `--eval NAME` replaces `--curated` and `--harbor`. Agentic and nonagentic suites launch as separate jobs, because an agentic launch serves the model's resolved serving config, which changes chat run IDs. A run's `concurrency` setting bounds attempts at once without entering its identity. The agent benchmarks use Harbor's 16 or 32, because at 64 Terminal-Bench attempts timed out under model latency. Judge specs gain ordered `candidate_steps` and a `sampling` table; specs without them keep their digests. Main removed `tau3-pi` and `sotopia-hard` in #11080, so the campaign no longer runs them. Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct ran each campaign evaluation on the curated path with `--limit 100`, with the campaign's vLLM configuration and Daytona sandboxes. The table compares those runs with the campaign's Harbor run of the same model. Terminal-Bench and TBLite run three trials per task, the others one. The paired difference is the per-task curated minus Harbor mean reward, with its standard error (SE) across tasks. Coverage is the share of curated attempts that were scored; Harbor scored at least 97.8%. | Evaluation | Paired tasks | Curated | Harbor | Difference (SE) | Coverage | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `tb2-recovery` | 87 | 0.115 | 0.107 | +0.008 (0.019) | 98.1% | | `ot-tblite-recovery` | 99 | 0.236 | 0.257 | −0.021 (0.026) | 99.0% | | `swebench-verified` | 100 | 0.250 | 0.260 | −0.010 (0.033) | 100% | | `ds-1000-local` | 100 | 0.210 | 0.170 | +0.040 (0.024) | 100% | | `bfclparity-pi` | 100 | 0.570 | 0.580 | −0.010 (0.048) | 100% | | `bixbench-pi` | 100 | 0.150 | 0.110 | +0.040 (0.024) | 100% | Every difference is within 2 SE. Terminal-Bench's unscored attempts failed when the Daytona organization reached its CPU limit. Archived OT-TBLite records show a 97.3-minute Harbor inference window and a 147.1-minute curated window with retries. Both used the same Qwen model, H100×2, and concurrency 16. The archived Harbor run used 73,728 input tokens, while curated used the checked-in policy’s 32,768. About 28 minutes of the difference accrued in the first pass and 22 around retries. First-pass vLLM queueing was negligible, with mean inter-token latency of 11.0 ms in Harbor and 8.85 ms in curated. [Harbor record](https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20260927-170244-Qwen-Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-ot-tblite-recovery-53b7) · [Curated record](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fevals%2F20261119-233653-Qwen-Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-84f95dab7c8e4c8b919aa8663c272e6a-ot-tblite-recovery-44d99520a3275903b28dd164b12afe9f%2Frecord.json) A single archive writer thread serializes durable records while the event loop continues processing model and sandbox I/O. The run waits for each durable transition and the writer drains before the archive closes. In a local 240-attempt profile, maximum event-loop lag fell from 3.77 seconds to 96 ms. In a matched OT-TBLite run with five tasks, three repeats, concurrency 16 and a 32,768-token input limit, Harbor took 32.2 minutes and curated took 31.8 minutes on its first pass. Both hit the agent deadline on the same task. Harbor graded the existing work. Curated lost its sandbox during cancelled Daytona command staging and reached 40.2 minutes after one retry. Both paths scored all 15 trials. The paired reward difference was +0.200 (SE 0.133). This run evaluated the archive writer and preceded the Daytona fix. A prelaunch cancellation now removes the staging files and keeps the sandbox available for grading. Cancellation after a launch request still requires confirmed process-group cleanup. [Harbor timing record](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fevals%2Fharbor-timing-20261124-ac71c1e4bc-ot-tblite-harbor-timing-9a47214e869a503d98b44e6cb242e8da%2Frecord.json) · [Curated timing record](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fevals%2Fharbor-timing-20261124-ac71c1e4bc-ot-tblite-recovery-861531ba9c5f577e852741da9dd4d050%2Frecord.json) A cold Terminal-Bench 2.1 corpus build still uses vendored Harbor to fetch the pinned Hub packages. #12167 replaces that fetch with direct acquisition. The standalone Harbor evaluation driver, the pending trial policy (#12147), and live SkyRL rollouts and checkpoint evaluations still depend on the vendored runtime. Historical record readers and policy identities need to survive its removal. --------- Co-authored-by: rjpower

[taskforge] Replace Taskforge with the effect-driven core (#11109)

Replace `lib/taskforge` with the core of the effect-driven rewrite,
keeping the package and distribution name (`taskforge`,
`marin-taskforge`). Every model call, shell command, file read and grade
becomes a typed effect, executed in a scope and recorded in an event
log. A crashed workpiece resumes by replay: model calls are read back
from the log, and commands run again on a fresh machine.

This PR removes the previous package: the staged pipeline, the ledger
and the agentic path under `taskforge/agentic`. It adds:

- `effects`: effect types, scopes, observers, the JSONL event log and
replay, and the `Transient`/`Restart`/`Hold`/`LogFailure` decisions.
- `model`: frozen proposal, workpiece, controls, review and verdict
models.
- `policy`: the policy record, its overlays and the default prompts.
- `resources`: replayable environments, inference, provider, execution,
rollouts, ids, clock, web and sandbox factories.
- `llm`: the GLM transport from the previous package (`client`,
`policy`, `glm_client`, `structured`, and their tests). `llm/wire.py`
keeps the two helpers the new code needs from the old `agent` and
`rollout_model` modules (`replay_arguments`, `model_turn`). The old
tests were annotated to meet this package's strict pyrefly rules.

Deleting the old package removes the experiments built on it.
`experiments/post_training/capability_driven_envs/` is removed in full
(17 files: `catalog.py`, `generate_tasks.py`,
`generate_tasks_agentic.py`, `program_prompt.py`, `example_program.py`,
`analyze_failed_runs/`, `data/example_catalog.json` and `tests/`). None
of the ten modules that imported `taskforge` has a direct equivalent in
the new core: they need `CapabilityIdea`, the old stage pipeline or the
agentic generator, and the remaining files in that directory were only
used by those modules.

The `taskforge-unit` CI suite now runs `pytest lib/taskforge/tests` and
pyrefly with the package's own config. Its triggers drop the capability
experiments and add `experiments/taskforge/`, finelog and finestore.
`taskforge` becomes a selector scope, so modules outside the package
that import it are traced.

This supersedes #10998 (wp0), #11000 (wp1), #11001 (wp2) and #10999
(wp3). The workspace package, CI selection, scoped effects with durable
typed replay, the replayable execution resources and the immutable
workpiece and policy contracts described in those PRs are here under the
`taskforge` name. The `taskforge.llm.glm_client` change from the
integration branch is included here.

Tests: 368 package tests and the `lib/shellbox` suite pass (the Iris
machine tests: 54 passed, 1 skipped), and package pyrefly, repository
pyrefly and pre-commit are clean.

Lines: +6,181 / −18,149 (net −11,968). `lib/taskforge` accounts for
15,737 of the deleted lines (the old package plus the rewritten
pyproject, README and AGENTS) and the capability experiments for 2,279.
The library changes are +462 / −78 in source and +585 / −27 in tests;
they include Iris uploads and downloads raising `GuestPathError` with
the guest's errno only when the guest refuses the caller's path, so the
file tools report it to the model while host-side and helper failures
stay infrastructure failures. Stack running total: net −11,968.

Follow-up: S3 output roots (`marin/forge/...`), Iris job prefixes
(`forge-pilot-*`), sandbox paths and the event-log markers
(`__forge_*__`) keep the `forge` names used by the live pilots on
`mark/forge-integration`. Events are logged under their module path, so
pilot logs written under `forge.*` do not replay under `taskforge.*`.

This PR targets main directly and carries the support-library changes
the new package calls, fitted to main's current behaviour:

- shellbox: typed machine failures (`MachineTerminated` for a closed or
dead container, `MachineResourceExhausted` and
`MachineOutputLimitExceeded`, `MachineCancelled`, `MachineUnavailable`,
`ExecSetupFailed`) raised by the Iris and ShellSim backends, plus
`CommandOutcomeUnknown` for an Iris command whose reply or output
capture was lost after the controller may have run it. Taskforge replays
the stage on a fresh sandbox for that case instead of retrying the
command in place. The same holds for a file write: a transfer helper
whose reply was lost may still truncate or append after a resend, so any
write failure other than a connection refused before sending restarts on
a fresh sandbox. One-to-three-file hydration writes file by file and is
covered; four-file hydration stages a fresh archive name per attempt and
is still retried in place, as are read-only helpers. Only two dispatch
failures show that the command was never sent, and only they are retried
in place: a connection refused before any request was written, and the
controller exec pool's admission refusal, matched by its exact text
because Iris gives it no typed detail. Every other dispatch failure may
follow execution. That includes the Kubernetes WebSocket setup-failure
text, which the client also reports after an exec whose upgrade reply
was lost, and a RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED from a reply above the client's size
limit. An exec error reply such as a lost Kubernetes exec stream and any
failure of the diagnostic status lookup yield `CommandOutcomeUnknown`,
or `MachineTerminated` when the status shows the sandbox gone. A failed
capture is also `CommandOutcomeUnknown`, unless a guest helper failed or
the sandbox is gone, which keep their hold or restart; a cleanup failure
or nonzero `rm` exit is logged without replacing the result or the
command's failure. Iris file reads and writes classify path faults in
the one exec that attempts them, with `sh` builtins and `test` and a
walk bounded by the path's depth; any other guest helper failure is
`GuestHelperFailed`, which Taskforge holds with its cause. A file read
of a directory is refused before anything is archived. The environment
and rollout resources choose restart, hold or retry from these types.
Iris `run()` also sends the command timeout as the exec deadline, since
without one the controller falls back to its 60 s Kubernetes default.
`IrisMachine.reset` lets the round verifier reuse one sandbox across
gradings; it stays in shellbox because it preserves the backend's own
capture files and closes the machine when it fails.
- rolloutengine: `run_task(verifier=...)`, through which the round
verifier lends its machine to an attempt.
- taskcompendium: `GRADER_EXIT` and `GRADER_TIMEOUT`, so a grader that
the author wrote wrongly returns to the author instead of counting as
lost infrastructure, and `ScriptGrader` reports an invalid judge spec as
a validation error.
- verifyit: `JudgeConnection.transport`, which the host judge uses to
route judge calls through the inference effect.

The rest of #11108 is not needed and stays out: the Iris Kubernetes
changes, retrying execs on any transport error, range reads, batched
staging, grader timing diagnostics, typed link failures and the shellsim
pin. The in-container command timeout and the NaN-tolerant digest live
in Taskforge instead, as does the authored-defect check, which arrives
with lowering in #11110.

[grug] Run AMD Pallas flash attention at any GQA ratio (#11927)

`gpu_pallas_triton_flash` now accepts any GQA ratio that divides the
query heads, not only powers of two. The Snowball d768 ladder rung (6
query heads, 1 KV head) can now use it instead of `xla_flash`, and its
step time halves on MI355X.

The power-of-two check was stricter than Triton needs. Pallas-Triton
requires power-of-two sizes only for the tiles a kernel loads and
stores, not for BlockSpec block shapes. The dK/dV kernel carries the
query-head group as a block dimension but loops over it in Python and
loads one `(block, head_dim)` tile per head, so a group of 6 lowers
as-is. Kernel code is unchanged, so outputs for power-of-two ratios are
bit-identical.

The parity tests now cover ratios 1, 2, 3, 6 and 8 under causal and
window masks, for forward and gradients. On MI355X the full test file
passes, including the default-tile production-shape test at 6:1,
compiled through Triton.

[scaling_laws] Add hinted scaling-law fits and their baselines (#11891)

Add `marin.scaling_laws.hinted_fit`, which forecasts a model's unhinted
benchmark accuracy from hinted scores on a smaller model ladder,
following Hinted Scaling Laws ([arXiv
2611.02270](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02270)). Each hint method
(truncation, masking) gets the joint law acc(C, H) = max(F, L + (A −
L)·σ(b1·(C − 20) + b2·H + b0)), where C is log10 training FLOPs and H is
hint strength. The forecast is the law at H = 0, and the hinted ensemble
averages the two methods. The module also fits the two baselines the
paper compares against: a sigmoid on unhinted scores, and a two-stage
compute → bits per byte → accuracy fit. `bootstrap_forecasts` resamples
benchmark problems with one shared draw across all cells and refits
every forecast.

The fits mirror the paper's code
([tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws@c0490e53](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/hinted-scaling-laws/tree/c0490e53ba8eae58bf5375f6b56956f0d57dad30),
`experiments/forecasting/plot.py` and `two_stage.py`): same
parameterization, bounds, 162 joint-law starts, and unweighted least
squares on cell accuracies. On the paper's released per-problem data,
the module reproduces:

- all ten Table 1 joint-law parameter sets (largest difference from the
printed values 0.0048);
- Table 1's in-sample MAE, 3.1 pp for masking and 3.3 pp for truncation;
- the Delphi GSM8K forecast errors for the 1e23 model to four decimals,
for 7 to 11 fitted rungs. With 9 rungs, the ensemble forecasts 0.253
(90% bootstrap interval 0.221–0.288) against an observed 0.259; the
sigmoid baseline gives 0.148 and the two-stage baseline 0.096;
- the two-stage baseline errors from `two_stage.py` exactly.

`bits_per_byte` is optional; without it the two-stage baseline is
skipped and left out of the forecasts.

The tests check the paper's numbers on six pairs: GSM8K × Delphi, AIME ×
Qwen2.5-Instruct and Qwen3, and HLE × Qwen2.5-Instruct, Qwen3 and
Qwen3.5.
- Table 1 slopes, intercepts and in-sample MAE, for the four of these
pairs that Table 1 prints.
- Sigmoid-baseline and ensemble forecast errors at every fitted size
`plot.py` prints, for all six pairs.
- Delphi two-stage errors.

Their inputs are `tests/scaling_laws/delphi_gsm8k_cells.json` (13 KB)
and `qwen_cells.json` (30 KB). These hold the paper's cell accuracies,
not rollouts or problems. The paper repository has no license file.
Table 1 is checked through MAE, not the lower asymptote and floor
parameters directly. Near zero accuracy those two trade off: perturbing
the inputs by 1e-8 moves the Delphi truncation floor by 0.001 without
changing the fitted curve. The paper code has no bootstrap. This one
resamples problems only, not training seeds, rollouts or bits per byte,
and takes about 1.5 s per resample. Its test checks that intervals cover
a known law's forecast and narrow as problems increase.

The module uses `scipy`, which `marin-core` already installs through
jax. Dependencies are unchanged.

Fixes #11867. Part of #9541; the Delphi validation gate in #11868 uses
these fits.
